props.title: Save the Tiger
props.initialSlug: Desperate businessman's moral crisis in 1970s LA

sections.content: **Save the Tiger** (1973) stands as one of the defining films about American disillusionment in the post-war era. Jack Lemmon delivers a career-best performance as Harry Stoner, a struggling garment manufacturer wrestling with moral decay and PTSD from WWII. The film captures the exact moment when the American Dream began to curdle, similar to how **The Graduate** (1967) depicted youth alienation and **Death of a Salesman** (1951) portrayed the crushing weight of capitalism on the individual. Director John G. Avildsen crafts a haunting portrait of a businessman's spiritual crisis that influenced later works like Glengarry Glen Ross (1992) and **Falling Down** (1993).

sections.content: The film's exploration of post-war trauma and business ethics created a template for examining American masculinity in crisis. Like **The Last Picture Show** (1971) and **Five Easy Pieces** (1970), it captures a distinctly American malaise. Harry Stoner's moral compromises - from tax fraud to arson - mirror the broader corruption of American values that would later explode in films like **Network** (1976) and **Wall Street** (1987). Lemmon's performance is particularly remarkable for how it balances desperation with dignity, creating a character study that influenced later works like **American Beauty** (1999). SUBHEAD: The Crisis of American Masculinity

**Save the Tiger** particularly resonates with its examination of male identity in crisis. Harry's flashbacks to WWII and his longing for an idealized past connect directly to films like **The Best Years of Our Lives** (1946) and **Coming Home** (1978). The film's Los Angeles setting becomes a character itself, presenting a sun-bleached nightmare similar to **The Long Goodbye** (1973) and **Chinatown** (1974). The way Harry moves through this landscape, increasingly disconnected from reality, established a pattern for character studies like **Taxi Driver** (1976) and **First Reformed** (2017).
